title: 88% of Young Americans Admit to Doomscrolling
paragraphs: Many young people spend hours scrolling through negative news and posts on social media, a habit known as "doomscrolling." According to a new survey, the habit is extremely common among young people, and it may be harming their sleep and mental health.

The survey was carried out by Hopelab, an organization that supports young people's mental health, together with the research group Data for Progress. It asked more than 1,400 people aged 13 to 24 about their social media habits. The results were reported in October 2026.

The survey found that 88% of the young people counted as doomscrollers. According to Mike Parent, the lead researcher at Hopelab, this was more than the researchers had expected. He also said that a huge number of young people were doing it every night or almost every night. The most common answer for how much sleep they lost to doomscrolling was more than an hour each time.

Doomscrolling also seemed to affect the young people's emotions. About six in ten said that it made them feel anxious, mentally exhausted, overwhelmed, angry or hopeless. According to Parent, social media feeds can push users toward more negative content, because negative emotional content gets more interaction. He also noted that LGBTQ+ young people may be particularly affected, because their feeds can be full of negative stories about violence and hateful comments.

Lack of sleep is a serious problem for young people. According to Dr. Amanda Hassinger of the UBMD Pediatric Sleep Center, not getting enough sleep can lead to higher rates of mental health problems. In addition, the light from phone screens can delay the release of melatonin, a hormone that helps people fall asleep.

Experts recommend putting phones away about an hour before going to bed. Hassinger also suggests setting a social media curfew and charging phones away from bedrooms. Meanwhile, Parent suggests replacing scrolling with calming activities, such as reading or writing in a journal.

Other surveys have found similar results. For example, a poll by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine in February 2026 found that 38% of American adults said reading the news on their phones before bed made their sleep worse.
